questions.q: What does dependency injection mean?
questions.explain: With dependency injection the class does not build its store or clock itself: the caller passes them in. That is why they can be shared between services and replaced in tests.
options: A class creates everything it needs with new inside its constructor
A class receives what it needs, usually as constructor parameters, instead of creating it
A class imports a global variable that holds all services
A class downloads its dependencies from npm when it starts

questions.q: A TaskService does new TaskStore() and new Date() inside itself. Why is it hard to test?
questions.explain: The service decides everything itself, so the test has no way in. Once the store and a clock are passed in, the test can pass a clock that always says the same date and check the exact output.
options: Classes that use new cannot be exported
The code does not compile in strict TypeScript
A test cannot give it an empty store or a fixed date, so the output changes every day
It is slower than a service built by a container

questions.q: What is the composition root?
questions.explain: Someone still has to call the constructors in the right order. Doing it in one place (in the Task API, src/container.ts) keeps the wiring out of the services themselves.
options: The one place in the app where you say how every service is built and connected
The first class in the inheritance chain
The service that every other service depends on

questions.q: Why can't an interface such as Clock be used directly as a container token?
questions.explain: TypeScript removes interfaces when it compiles. A class does exist at runtime, so it can be its own token; an interface needs a token made with createToken<Clock>("Clock").
options: Interfaces are always too big to store in a Map
Interfaces only exist for TypeScript; they are gone when the program runs, so there is nothing to use as a key
Interfaces can only be used with registerFactory

questions.q: Why does the lesson prefer createToken<number>("MaxTasks") over a plain string token like "maxTasks"?
questions.explain: With a string, resolve<number>("clock") compiles even if "clock" holds a clock object. A token made with createToken<T> carries its type, so resolve returns a T.
options: String tokens are slower to look up
String tokens are removed when the program runs
TypeScript knows the type behind a created token, but cannot check what a string token holds

questions.q: What does container.registerExisting(LOGGER, AppLogger) do?
questions.explain: registerExisting is an alias provider. If AppLogger is a singleton, both tokens give you the very same object.
options: It creates a second, separate AppLogger for LOGGER
It deletes the AppLogger registration and moves it to LOGGER
It makes LOGGER an alias: resolving it answers with whatever AppLogger resolves to
It checks that AppLogger is registered and throws if not

questions.q: registerClass(TaskService, TaskService, { inject: [TaskStore, CLOCK] }). Which habit does the lesson recommend for inject lists?
questions.explain: The tokens are passed to the constructor by position, in the order you list them. A small test that resolves every service catches a wrong list before users do.
options: Sort the tokens alphabetically so they are easy to find
Leave inject out; the container reads the constructor types
Keep the list in the same order as the constructor, and have a test that resolves every service once
Put the tokens in any order; the container matches them by name

questions.q: You register a class without a scope option. What lifetime does it get?
questions.explain: Transient is the default. If a service must be shared (a store, a pool, an id generator), say scope: ContainerScope.SINGLETON yourself.
options: Singleton: one instance for the whole container
Transient: a new instance on every resolve
None: registering without a scope throws an error

questions.q: A RequestContext holds data about one HTTP request (who is calling, the request id). Which lifetime fits?
questions.explain: Scoped means one instance per createScope(). Everything inside one request shares it, and the next request gets a fresh one. A singleton would mix different users' data.
options: ContainerScope.TRANSIENT, so every class gets its own copy
It should not be registered in a container at all

questions.q: Why does the container refuse a singleton that depends on a scoped dependency (CaptiveDependencyError)?
questions.explain: A singleton lives as long as the container. If it captured one request's RequestInfo, every later request would read that first request's data: a real data leak. The rule: a dependency must live at least as long as the thing that uses it.
options: Singletons are not allowed to have any dependencies
Scoped objects cannot be passed to constructors
The singleton would keep the first request's object forever, so later requests would see another user's data
It would create too many objects and use too much memory

questions.q: Which of these registrations is allowed?
questions.explain: A transient object is created for the request and never outlives it, so it may use a scoped dependency. The singleton case is a CaptiveDependencyError, resolving scoped without a scope is a ScopedResolutionError, and a second registration is a DuplicateRegistrationError.
options: A transient AuditLog that depends on a scoped RequestContext, resolved inside a scope
A singleton TaskService that depends on a scoped RequestContext
A scoped RequestContext resolved directly from the root container, with no scope
Two registrations for the same token, made with registerClass

questions.q: TaskService needs Notifier, and Notifier needs TaskService. The container throws CircularDependencyError. What is a good fix?
questions.explain: A cycle is a design problem, not a container problem: neither class can be built first, whatever the lifetime. Break the loop by pulling the shared logic out, or by publishing an event instead of calling the other class directly.
options: Make both classes singletons, so they are built only once
Catch the error and resolve the classes again
Move the shared part into a third class that both use, or let one side send an event

questions.q: Which objects does await container.dispose() call dispose() on?
questions.explain: The container cleans up what it created and kept: its singletons (and a scope cleans up its scoped objects). Transients are not tracked, and values from registerValue were not created by the container, so it does not own them.
options: Every object that was ever resolved, including transients
The singletons the container created itself, newest first
None: you must call dispose() on each object yourself

questions.q: Why does the container dispose singletons newest first?
questions.explain: A service is created after its dependencies, so newest first means "users before the things they use". The service can still flush its work through the pool, then the pool closes.
options: It is the fastest order for a Map
So a service is disposed before the pool it uses, while the pool is still open
So errors are printed in alphabetical order
Because the oldest objects are already garbage-collected

questions.q: In the Task API, when should you dispose the container?
questions.explain: The runtime does not dispose the container for you. Modules may still use services while they stop, so the container is disposed last.
options: At the very end of shutdown, after runtime.stop()

questions.q: In a test you want the real TaskNotifier but a fake MAILER that is already registered. What should you do?
questions.explain: Registering the same token twice is a DuplicateRegistrationError, on purpose, so a typo cannot silently replace a real service. replace says you mean it, and singletons built on the old mailer are rebuilt.
options: Edit TaskNotifier so it checks a TEST flag
Create a new token with the same name "Mailer"

questions.q: In the Task API schema, why write schema.enum(["low", "normal", "high"] as const)?
questions.explain: as const keeps the exact strings, so Infer gives "low" | "normal" | "high", which fits the store's Priority type. It is about the TypeScript type, not the runtime check.
options: Without as const the schema accepts any string at runtime
Without it, TypeScript widens the list to string[], so the inferred priority type is any string
as const makes the list faster to search
as const freezes the task object after parsing

questions.q: A route in the Task API needs the TaskService. How should it get it?
questions.explain: The runtime's container holds the singleton service that shares the one store. Calling new, or resolving from a brand-new container, would give the route a second store that the rest of the app never sees.
options: new TaskService(new TaskStore(), clock) inside the route

questions.explain: Every createToken call makes a new, unique token, even with the same name. The second token was never registered, so has is false.

questions.explain: A value provider hands out the exact object you registered, not a copy. So a and settings are the same object.

questions.explain: With no scope option the lifetime is transient: every resolve calls new Report() again. Two resolves, two objects.

questions.q: An id generator is registered without a scope. What does this print?
questions.explain: Transient is the default, so each resolve gives a new generator that starts at 0. Two tasks would get the same id 1: an id generator must be a singleton.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Scoped means one instance per scope. Inside request1 you always get the same object; request2 has its own.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A singleton stays the same everywhere, even when you resolve it through a scope. Only scoped registrations get a new object per scope.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A scoped dependency belongs to a request, so asking the root container for it (with no scope) fails with ScopedResolutionError. Resolve it through container.createScope().

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A singleton may not depend on a scoped object: it would capture one request's data forever. Resolving through a scope does not help, because the singleton would still outlive that scope.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The container notices the loop instead of recursing forever, and the message names the whole loop, from Orders back to Orders.
options: true Circular dependency detected: Orders -> Billing -> Orders.
false Maximum call stack size exceeded
true Circular dependency detected: Orders -> Billing.

questions.q: The inject list is written in the wrong order. What does this print?
questions.explain: The container passes the resolved tokens to the constructor by position, in the order of inject. It does not match them by name, so the arguments arrive swapped. Keep the list in the same order as the constructor.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The factory's third argument lists the tokens to inject. The container resolves START (41) and calls the factory with it, so the result is task #42.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: registerExisting makes an alias. LOGGER answers with whatever AppLogger resolves to, and that is a singleton, so both give the same object.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Registering the same token twice by accident is an error, so a typo cannot silently replace a real service. When you really want to swap it, call replace.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Nothing was registered for MAILER, so resolve throws RegistrationNotFoundError. It does not quietly return undefined.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The pool was created first (the service needed it), so disposing newest first stops the service before its pool is closed.
options:
service stopped
pool closed
disposed: true

pool closed
service stopped
disposed: true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Disposing a scope only disposes that scope's objects. The singleton pool belongs to the container and stays open until container.dispose().
options:
request log flushed
pool closed
--- request finished

pool closed
request log flushed
--- request finished

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The container did not create a value from registerValue, so it does not own it and never disposes it. Whoever created cache must clean it up.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: replace swaps the mailer, and the singleton Notifier that was built on the old one is rebuilt. So the second message goes to the fake, which records it instead of sending it.
options:
SMTP: Buy milk is done
[ 'Walk the dog is done' ]

SMTP: Buy milk is done
SMTP: Walk the dog is done
[]

SMTP: Buy milk is done
[ 'Buy milk is done', 'Walk the dog is done' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: snapshot() saves the registrations, replace swaps in the fake, and restoreSnapshot puts the real one back, just like the end of a test.

questions.q: Create a token called CLOCK with createToken, register the fixed clock object as its value, and resolve it into clock. The program should print 2026-09-23.
questions.explain: createToken("Clock") names the dependency, registerValue hands out the object you give it, and resolve(CLOCK) gets it back.

questions.q: Register TaskStore and TaskService so the container can build the service. TaskService receives the store and then the clock, so its inject list must be [TaskStore, CLOCK]. The program should print #1 Buy milk at 09:00.
questions.explain: A class can be its own token: registerClass(TaskStore, TaskStore). The inject list gives the constructor arguments in order, so the container calls new TaskService(store, clock) for you.

questions.q: The id generator is registered as transient, so both calls print 1. Change the registration so the whole container shares one generator. The program should print 1 2.
questions.explain: Add { scope: ContainerScope.SINGLETON }. Now both resolves return the same generator, so the second call continues from 1.

questions.q: Register a factory for BASE_URL that receives HOST and PORT (in that order) and returns http://HOST:PORT. The program should print http://localhost:3000.
questions.explain: registerFactory(token, fn, inject): the container resolves the inject tokens and passes them to your function in the same order, then uses what it returns.

questions.q: Register RequestContext as scoped. Then create two scopes, first and second, with container.createScope(). The program should print true false: the same object inside one request, different objects in two requests.
questions.explain: ContainerScope.SCOPED gives one instance per scope. In a real server you create one scope per HTTP request, so each request gets its own context.

questions.q: This registration throws CaptiveDependencyError: a singleton AuditLog depends on a scoped RequestContext. Change only the AuditLog lifetime so it can never outlive a request. The program should print req-1 req-2.
questions.explain: A dependency must live at least as long as the thing that uses it. Making AuditLog scoped (transient also works) means each request gets a log bound to its own context, so no data leaks between requests.

questions.q: Give Pool a dispose() method that prints pool closed, so the container cleans it up. The program should print pool closed and then disposed: true.
questions.explain: An object is disposable if it has a dispose() method. container.dispose() calls it on every singleton the container created.

questions.q: In this test, replace MAILER with a fake whose send(text) pushes the text into sent instead of printing SMTP. Use container.replace. The program should print [ 'Buy milk is done' ].
questions.explain: replace(MAILER, { useValue: fake }) swaps the registration. Notifier does not change at all, and the test can inspect exactly what would have been sent.

questions.q: Make LOGGER an alias for the singleton AppLogger with registerExisting. The program should print true.
questions.explain: registerExisting(LOGGER, AppLogger) answers LOGGER with whatever AppLogger resolves to. Because AppLogger is a singleton, both tokens give the same object.

questions.q: Finish registerServices, the composition root. Register CLOCK as a value, TaskStore as a singleton, and TaskService as a singleton that injects [TaskStore, CLOCK]. The program should print 1 true.
questions.explain: Both must be singletons: the service wrote to the store, and resolve(TaskStore) sees that task only because it is the same shared store. A transient store would print 0.
